newsitem.title: USA: Shareholders OK Boeing, McDonnell Douglas merger.
newsitem.headline: Shareholders OK Boeing, McDonnell Douglas merger.

text.p: Boeing Co. shareholders on Friday approved the company's proposed $16 billion acquisition of longtime rival McDonnell Douglas Corp., clearing the way for the deal to be closed next week.
At a separate meeting in St. Louis, McDonnell Douglas shareholders also approved the transaction.
"Today I believe we have been part of making history," Boeing Chief Executive Phil Condit told the meeting.
"I believe that by working together we will, this company will, define the future of flight," he told a room full of shareholders in Seattle.

"Our merger with Boeing represents the best, even the ideal, solution for the future, for our customers, teammates and shareholders," McDonnell Douglas Chairman John McDonnell told the special shareholder meeting in St. Louis.
The votes came two days after Boeing scrapped exclusive sales deals and made other concessions to win European Commission approval for the merger, clearing the biggest obstacle to the plan.
The merger plan was announced in December and quickly backed by the Pentagon, which has encouraged consolidation of military contractors.

The U.S. Federal Trade Commission already had granted unconditional approval to the deal, which will create the nation's biggest aerospace company, with projected sales this year of more than $38 billion.
Shareholder approval clears the way for the deal to close Aug. 1, and the companies will begin operating as a single entity in 27 states.
Shareholder approval was a mere formality after Boeing and officials of the European Union went to the brink of a trans-Atlantic trade war before cutting a deal hours before the EC vote.

At a news conference after the shareholder meeting, Condit said he expected "relatively modest rises" in employment going forward and that the merger itself would not have a major effect on the job picture.
He said he thought most of the company's major hiring to meet the increased demand for airplanes was behind it.
Condit said employment at Boeing had risen by about 1,900 jobs over the past month to slightly more than 159,000, compared with 147,600 at the end of last year.
The acquisition of the McDonnell Douglas will add about 60,000 jobs.
Condit said there were "possibilities" the company would move some commerical production work to McDonnell Douglas' underused facilities in Long Beach, Calif.
He said it was unlikely that Boeing would move any final assembly work to California but that the company could benefit from a new source of parts production.

Condit said he expected orders this year to be in the same order of magnitude as last year's record level. He said the current airline industry order rate was sustainable, unlike in the late 1980s, when the last order cycle peaked.
Condit also said the company's employee stock plan likely would be extended to employees who join Boeing in the merger.
Harry Stonecipher, chief executive officer of McDonnell Douglas, said the combined company was committed to the Douglas Aircraft commercial airline unit.
"We will continue to manufacture commercial aircraft," Stonecipher said at the shareholder meeting.
It will take "a year to a year and half to fully integrate," the two companies, he said, adding that he did not know the total costs of the merger.
